title: The Polio Vaccine Field Trial
text:
In the early 1950s polio struck tens of thousands of American children every summer, leaving many paralyzed. Jonas Salk, at the University of Pittsburgh, had developed a killed-virus vaccine, but it had to be tested on a scale never tried before. The National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis, funded by the March of Dimes, in which ordinary Americans mailed in coins, organized the trial and paid for it.

The trial was run independently of Salk by Thomas Francis Jr., an epidemiologist at the University of Michigan, who insisted on a rigorous design. In 1954 about 1.8 million schoolchildren in the United States, Canada and Finland took part. In some areas children were randomly given either vaccine or an identical-looking placebo, with neither the families nor the doctors knowing which. In others, second graders were vaccinated and compared with other grades. The children received buttons and certificates calling them Polio Pioneers.

The effort depended on huge numbers of volunteers: doctors and nurses giving injections, teachers and parents organizing schools, local clubs keeping records. Francis's team then spent almost a year analyzing the data.

On 12 April 1955, in Ann Arbor, Francis announced the results: the vaccine was safe and effective. Church bells rang in some towns. Within hours the government licensed the vaccine, and mass vaccination began.
lesson: Some answers need a whole community working carefully together. Big efforts succeed when many people do small, well-defined tasks and an independent team checks the results.
people: Jonas Salk, Thomas Francis Jr., National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis, the Polio Pioneers
location: United States, Canada and Finland; analysis at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, USA
source: Thomas Francis Jr. et al., Evaluation of the 1954 Field Trial of Poliomyelitis Vaccine: Final Report (1957); David M. Oshinsky, Polio: An American Story (2005)
